name: The transformation of man's place in the universe
plain_explanation: In the medieval picture, the earth sat at the center of a cosmos designed around human concerns. Once Copernicus, Kepler, and Newton showed the earth to be a minor planet of an unremarkable star in an immense mechanical universe, it became hard to believe the whole apparatus existed for the sake of small creatures on a 'pin-point' -- yet, paradoxically, the very triumphs of science that should have humbled humanity instead revived human pride and self-satisfaction.
precise_definition: Russell's account of the double effect: the Copernican and Newtonian universe 'should have been humbling to human pride, but in fact the contrary effect was produced, for the triumphs of science revived human pride,' displacing the earlier medieval 'sense of sin' with confidence exemplified by Pope's couplet, 'Nature and Nature's laws lay hid in night. / God said "Let Newton be," and all was light.'
why_it_mattered: It illustrates a recurring irony in intellectual history that Russell highlights: a discovery that logically diminishes human cosmic importance can psychologically and culturally increase human self-confidence, especially when combined with contemporaneous European commercial and imperial expansion.
historical_origin: A cumulative cultural effect of the astronomical and physical discoveries recounted through the chapter, reaching its clearest expression by the later seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries.
examples: European material and imperial self-satisfaction (conquest of the Americas, influence in Africa, India, China, Japan) as a parallel, non-scientific source of the same growing self-confidence
competing_positions: The medieval theological outlook, in which humility before God was 'both right and prudent, for God would punish pride'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly concerns the theological doctrine of sin and damnation, which Russell suggests became harder to sustain in full medieval severity once human intellectual achievement seemed so impressive.
